title: This faraway planet has rock clouds that disappear every night!
summary:
Imagine waking up to a sky filled with clouds made of tiny rock crystals. By lunchtime, the heat is so intense that the clouds simply vanish—poof! That's a typical day on WASP-94A b, a giant planet almost 700 light-years away. Using NASA's super-powerful James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers just watched this incredible weather cycle happen in real time.

WASP-94A b is what scientists call a "Hot Jupiter"—a gas giant that orbits scorchingly close to its star. It's so close that one side always faces the star and gets crazy hot, while the other side is in permanent darkness. The telescope caught the planet as it passed in front of its star, letting scientists peek at its morning and evening edges separately. What they found was a huge surprise: the morning side was packed with clouds, but the evening side was almost completely clear!

What are these clouds made of? Magnesium silicate—a mineral that's common in rocks right here on Earth. So yes, it's literally rock clouds! Scientists think there are two reasons they disappear. Either powerful winds drag the clouds deep into the planet where we can't see them, or the clouds simply evaporate as they drift into the blazing 1,000-degree day side. It's like morning fog burning off on a hot summer day, but way more extreme.

This discovery is a big deal because clouds on exoplanets usually block our view, like trying to see through a foggy window. But the clear evening skies gave astronomers a crystal-clear look at the planet's atmosphere. They even solved an old mystery: earlier measurements made it seem like the planet had way too much oxygen and carbon, but now they know it's actually pretty similar to our own Jupiter. The team also found similar cloud cycles on two other Hot Jupiters. Next, they'll search even more planets for these wild weather patterns!
why_it_matters: Studying wild weather on other planets helps scientists understand how atmospheres behave, which might one day teach us more about Earth's own climate.

keywords.explanation: WASP-94A b is a distant giant planet where scientists watched rock clouds vanish each day.
A Hot Jupiter is a gas giant planet that orbits so close to its star that it gets extremely hot.
This is NASA's most powerful space telescope, launched to see faraway stars, galaxies, and planets in incredible detail.
Magnesium silicate is a common rock mineral on Earth that, on this planet, forms actual clouds high in the sky.
Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars outside our own solar system.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year—about 6 trillion miles—used to measure huge distances in space.

background_read: Hot Jupiters like WASP-94A b are gas giant planets that orbit very close to their stars, making them some of the first exoplanets ever discovered because they cause noticeable dips in starlight.
The James Webb Space Telescope (the largest and most powerful space telescope, launched in 2021) studies these distant worlds by analyzing starlight that shines through their atmospheres.
WASP-94A b is in the constellation Pegasus, and the light we see from it left the planet 700 years ago, so we are watching its weather as it was in the Middle Ages.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.
WHAT: They observed that WASP-94A b has clouds of rock crystals that form on the morning side and vanish by the evening.
WHERE: On the exoplanet WASP-94A b, about 700 light-years from Earth.
WHY: To understand how weather works on other worlds and to solve the puzzle of earlier measurements that seemed off.

perspectives.perspective: Positive – A glimpse of alien skies
perspectives.description: Seeing rock clouds vanish in real time is an exciting breakthrough that shows we can now watch weather on planets trillions of miles away.

perspectives.perspective: Critical – Clouds often spoil the view
perspectives.description: Normally, clouds block our ability to study exoplanet atmospheres, but the clear evenings on WASP-94A b gave a lucky window; many other planets remain hidden.
The team found similar cloud cycles on two other Hot Jupiters, hinting that this might be a common weather pattern in the universe.
